items.prompt: A report holds the cart as `a`, and the preview holds the same cart as `b`. The preview runs `b.total = 45`. What does the report print for `a.total`?

items.prompt: What does a function do if it follows the immutable style?
choices: Edits the argument it was given in place
Returns a new object with the change
items.explanation: The change is built into a new value and the original is left alone.

items.explanation: Nothing wrote to the original, so it keeps its value.

items.prompt: Which expression builds a new object with a changed total?
items.explanation: A spread with an override makes a new object; assignments edit the old one.

items.prompt: Why is a preview easy with a returning function?

items.explanation: The preview works on a separate result and can be dropped.

No, names point to new values

items.explanation: Other holders still point at the original.

items.prompt: Which approach lets a user undo a change easily?
items.explanation: If the old object still exists, undo is just pointing back at it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a mutation?
items.explanation: Assigning to a property of an existing object edits it in place.

items.prompt: The preview must show a discounted total without affecting checkout. Which design achieves that?
choices: Edit the cart, then edit it back on cancel
Lock the cart while the preview is open
Return a new cart and show that one only
Run the promo function twice to cancel itself
items.explanation: Only a new object guarantees the real cart was never touched, so nothing needs undoing.
items.reference:
Edit in place or return a new one
✏️ mutating: the original changes for everyone
🆕 new object: the original is untouched
👀 the caller that keeps the result sees the change
💳 other holders see the old value until swapped
Why: returning a new object limits the change to whoever asks for it.
items.learnMore:
Immutability

Treat data as unchanging once made. A function that needs a different value returns a new one, so previews, undo and comparisons all get a safe 'before' to look at.

Common mistake

Thinking immutability means nothing can ever change; the program still changes by swapping which value a name points to.

It works only for carts that hold a single line item
items.explanation: Between the two edits another reader can observe the changed cart, and a crash can skip the undo.

items.prompt: Which function is pure?
items.explanation: Only the first depends solely on inputs and changes nothing else.

items.prompt: A function returns `Date.now() + x`. Is it pure?
items.explanation: Same input at different times gives different output.

items.prompt: Which counts as a side effect?
items.explanation: Changing something outside the function is a side effect.

items.prompt: A function uses `const` and an arrow but runs `cart.total *= 0.9`. Pure?
items.explanation: Syntax does not matter; the edit is a side effect.

items.prompt: Calling a pure function twice with the same arguments gives...
choices: An error on the second call
items.explanation: That is what the same-input-same-output property says.

items.prompt: Which is easiest to test with no setup?
choices: A function that reads a file
items.explanation: Plain inputs and outputs need no mocks.

items.prompt: Does a `console.log` inside a function make it impure?
items.explanation: Printing changes the outside world, even if gently.

items.prompt: Which pair describes purity?
items.explanation: Purity is about repeatability and not changing anything else.

items.prompt: A function filters orders with `orders.filter(o => { o.seen = true; return o.total > 10; })`. Why is it not pure?
choices: Filter always creates side effects when it runs
Arrow callbacks cannot return a boolean value
The total comparison depends on the current clock
The callback edits each order it receives
items.explanation: The functional-looking call hides an assignment into the caller's objects.
items.reference:
Pure or not?
✅ same input gives same output
✅ edits nothing it was given
❌ reads the clock or a random number
❌ writes a file, calls a network, logs
Why: a pure function can be called, or called just to see, with no consequences.
items.learnMore:
Purity is behavior

A function is pure when its output depends only on its inputs and it changes nothing outside itself. Arrow syntax and const say nothing about either property.

Common mistake

Believing that code using map and arrow functions is automatically pure.

items.explanation: Effects stay at the edge so the core stays pure.

items.prompt: What does the core of the pattern contain?
items.explanation: The core only takes data in and returns data out.

items.prompt: Which direction do calls go?
items.explanation: The core must not reach out, or it stops being pure.

items.prompt: Why is the core easy to test?
choices: It needs no database or mocks
items.explanation: Plain inputs and outputs are all a test needs.

items.prompt: A function both computes a total and saves it. What is the fix?

items.explanation: A pure compute plus a thin save separates the concerns.

items.prompt: Can a real program avoid side effects completely?
choices: No, it must save or send
items.explanation: Effects are the purpose of most programs; they must be isolated, not removed.

items.prompt: Which function belongs in the shell?
items.explanation: Saving is the effect, so it belongs at the edge.

items.prompt: Which task could the core handle for a preview?
items.explanation: Only pure calculation is safe to run just to look.

items.prompt: A `computeAndSaveTotal(cart, db)` function is hard to reuse for a preview. What is the structural reason?
choices: It uses a loop instead of using recursion
It returns a number instead of an object
It has two parameters instead of just one
The calculation is welded to a database write
items.explanation: Any caller wanting only the number must also accept the write or duplicate the math.
items.reference:
Where each kind of code lives
🧮 core: pure calculation, totals, discounts
🐚 shell: reads input, saves, sends
↔️ shell calls core; core never calls the shell
🧪 core tests need no database
Why: pushing effects to the edge keeps the logic cheap to test and safe to reuse.
items.learnMore:
Functional core, imperative shell

Side effects cannot be removed, only placed. Put them in a thin outer layer that gathers data, calls pure code, then saves or sends the result.

Common mistake

Seeing the split as extra ceremony; it is what lets the same calculation serve a preview, a report and a checkout.

items.reference:
What a spread copies
🔢 numbers and strings: copied as values
🏹 nested arrays: same arrow, not a new array
🏹 nested objects: same arrow, not a new object
🌿 rebuild each level on the path you change
Why: a spread is one level deep; nested data stays shared.

items.explanation: Only the changed path is rebuilt.

items.explanation: Cost scales with size and only matters when the list is huge.

items.prompt: Is a full copy per update free?
items.explanation: Copying does real work, small at small sizes.

items.explanation: Benchmarks vary across machines and runs.

items.prompt: Should you decide on copying strategy before measuring?
items.explanation: Size and update rate decide whether it matters.

items.prompt: Using the demo's model (about 0.0000085 ms per item plus 0.001 ms), roughly how long does copying a 1,000-item list take?
items.reference:
Cost of a full copy (rough Node estimate)
10 items: about 0.001 ms
1,000 items: about 0.0095 ms
200,000 items: about 1.7 ms (10% of a 16.6 ms frame)
🌿 structural sharing: rebuild only the path to the change
Why: copy cost grows with list size; sharing the unchanged parts avoids paying for all of it.
items.learnMore:
Structural sharing

A new version reuses every piece that did not change and builds new boxes only on the path to the change. Cost then depends on how deep the change is, not how big the whole list is.

Common mistake

Concluding that immutability is too slow, or that it is always free; the answer depends on size and how often you update.

Structural sharing

A new version reuses every piece that did not change and builds new boxes only on the path to the change. Cost then depends on how deep the change is, not how big the whole list is.

Common mistake

Concluding that immutability is too slow, or that it is always free; the answer depends on size and how often you update.
items.reflection: When have you re-copied a whole thing to change one part? What would 'copy only the changed page' look like in that case?

items.prompt: One item in a large list changes. What does structural sharing rebuild?
choices: Only the path from the root to the changed item
The entire list and every item stored inside it
Only the changed item, leaving the list as it was
Nothing at all, because the old one is edited
items.explanation: The changed item and the containers above it get new boxes; everything else is reused.
items.reference:
Cost of a full copy (rough Node estimate)
10 items: about 0.001 ms
1,000 items: about 0.0095 ms
200,000 items: about 1.7 ms (10% of a 16.6 ms frame)
🌿 structural sharing: rebuild only the path to the change
Why: copy cost grows with list size; sharing the unchanged parts avoids paying for all of it.

items.prompt: A settings list holds 40 entries and changes once a minute. What is the sensible choice?
choices: A persistent data structure library at once
Mutate in place to avoid any copying
A plain copy, since the cost is negligible
Delay the update until idle time
items.explanation: At that size and rate, copying costs nothing noticeable; extra machinery would not pay for itself.

items.prompt: Implement `withTotal(cart, total)`: return a NEW cart object with the same properties and the given `total`. The original cart must not change.

tests.expr: expect(withTotal({ total: 50, items: [] }, 45).total).toBe(45)
expect((() => { const c = { total: 50 }; withTotal(c, 45); return c.total; })()).toBe(50)
expect((() => { const c = { total: 50 }; return withTotal(c, 45) === c; })()).toBe(false)

items.explanation: A spread copies the cart's properties into a new object and the later `total` overrides the copied one. The original is never assigned to.

items.prompt: Implement `withItem(items, item)`: return a NEW array containing the existing items followed by `item`. Do not use `push` on the original.

tests.expr: expect(withItem([1, 2], 3)).toEqual([1, 2, 3])
expect((() => { const a = [1, 2]; withItem(a, 3); return a.length; })()).toBe(2)

items.explanation: Spreading the array into a new array literal and adding the item builds a new list; the original array is never pushed to.

items.prompt: Implement `withoutLast(items)`: return a NEW array with every item except the last. Do not use `pop` on the original.

tests.expr: expect(withoutLast([1, 2, 3])).toEqual([1, 2])
expect((() => { const a = [1, 2, 3]; withoutLast(a); return a.length; })()).toBe(3)

items.explanation: slice returns a new array and never edits the one it is called on, unlike pop.

items.prompt: Implement `markDone(item)`: return a NEW item object with `done` set to true. The original item must stay as it was.

tests.expr: expect(markDone({ name: 'a', done: false }).done).toBe(true)
expect((() => { const i = { name: 'a', done: false }; markDone(i); return i.done; })()).toBe(false)

items.explanation: The spread copies the item and the override sets done on the copy only.

items.prompt: Implement `toggleItemDone(items, id)`: return a NEW array where the item with that `id` has `done` flipped. Every other item must be the SAME object as before, and the original array and items must not change.

tests.expr: expect(toggleItemDone([{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }], 2)).toEqual([{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: true }])

tests.description: does not edit the original item
tests.expr: expect((() => { const a = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; toggleItemDone(a, 1); return a[0].done; })()).toBe(false)
expect((() => { const a = [{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }]; return toggleItemDone(a, 2)[0] === a[0]; })()).toBeTruthy()
expect((() => { const a = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; return toggleItemDone(a, 1) === a; })()).toBe(false)

items.explanation: map builds the new array. The matching item is replaced by a spread copy with done flipped, and every other item is returned as-is, which keeps them shared and untouched.
items.reference:
Copy the path, share the rest
🆕 return a new array: map or filter, not push or assign
🔁 matching item: return a changed copy of it
♻️ other items: return the same object
🧪 check: the original is unchanged afterwards
Why: an update that builds new boxes only where needed leaves every other holder safe.
items.learnMore:
Immutable updates

map builds a new array; inside it, return a spread copy for the item to change and the item itself for the rest. The original array and items are never assigned into.

Common mistake

Writing items[i].done = true inside a map callback; it edits the original item and defeats the point.
items.reflection: Pick a thing you keep a list of (tasks, bookmarks, contacts). How would you let someone 'try' a change without losing the original list?

items.prompt: Implement `updateItemQty(items, id, qty)`: return a NEW array where the item with that `id` has `qty` set to the given value. Other items must be the same objects, and the original must not change.

tests.expr: expect(updateItemQty([{ id: 1, qty: 1 }, { id: 2, qty: 5 }], 1, 3)).toEqual([{ id: 1, qty: 3 }, { id: 2, qty: 5 }])

tests.description: does not edit the original item
tests.expr: expect((() => { const a = [{ id: 1, qty: 1 }]; updateItemQty(a, 1, 9); return a[0].qty; })()).toBe(1)
expect((() => { const a = [{ id: 1, qty: 1 }, { id: 2, qty: 5 }]; return updateItemQty(a, 1, 3)[1] === a[1]; })()).toBeTruthy()

items.explanation: The same copy-the-match, share-the-rest shape: map plus a spread with the override for the one matching item.

items.prompt: Implement `updateItemPrice(cart, id, price)`: return a NEW cart where the line item in `cart.items` with that `id` has `price` set. Rebuild the cart, the items array and that one item; the original cart must not change and other line items must be the same objects.

tests.expr: expect(updateItemPrice({ total: 50, items: [{ id: 1, price: 12 }, { id: 2, price: 8 }] }, 1, 10).items[0].price).toBe(10)
expect(updateItemPrice({ total: 50, items: [{ id: 1, price: 12 }] }, 1, 10).total).toBe(50)
expect((() => { const c = { total: 50, items: [{ id: 1, price: 12 }] }; updateItemPrice(c, 1, 10); return c.items[0].price; })()).toBe(12)
expect((() => { const c = { total: 50, items: [{ id: 1, price: 12 }, { id: 2, price: 8 }] }; return updateItemPrice(c, 1, 10).items[1] === c.items[1]; })()).toBeTruthy()

items.explanation: Each level on the path to the change gets a new object: the cart, the items array, and the one line item. Everything else is reused, so nested data is never shared in a way that lets the original be edited.

Why: an update that builds new boxes only where needed leaves every other holder safe.
